newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico Cetes rate drops on hopes of FOMC inaction.
newsitem.headline: Mexico Cetes rate drops on hopes of FOMC inaction.

text.p: Mexican overnight Cetes rates were down 245 basis points in mid-morning trade on Wednesday to 19.30 percent.

Fixed-income analysts said the sharp fall came in reponse to greater market liquidity following recent month-end pressures, confidence the Federal Open Market Committee was not about to raise U.S. interest rates, and the outlook for smooth mid-term elections on July 6.
"We expect the FOMC not to raise U.S. base rates, and that has calmed the market," one analyst said.
The FOMC was expected to announce its decision at 1315 local time/1815 GMT, or shortly before the close of trade on the Mexican money market.
"The approaching mid-term elections are no longer having an impact on the market... There is a lot of liquidity around today," the analyst added.

Mexicans vote on Sunday for an new lower house of congress, a quarter of the senate, six state governors and, for the first time, mayor of Mexico City. Previously, Mexico City's mayor was hand-picked by the president.
Dealers said market calm ahead of the elections explained an unexpected fall in domestic primary rates at Tuesday night's central bank auction.

Banco de Mexico placed bellwether 28-day Cetes at 19.95 percent at the auction, a fall of 95 basis points since last week. This compares with an average rise of 18 basis points predicted in a previously conducted Reuters survey.
Dealers remarked on heavy foreign demand for paper, which was also in evidence at the primary auction, where the overall bid-to-cover ratio was 5.53, up from 4.78 the week before.
Overnight rates on bank paper paralleled government rates and fell 220 basis points to 21.20 percent.
Liquidity of 1.231 billion pesos was due to return to the system from prior central bank operations.
"The international community favours greater participation by opposition parties in Congress," another dealer said.
Mexicans vote on Sunday for an new lower house of Congress, a quarter of the Senate, six state governors and, for the first time, a mayor of Mexico City.
Political analysts say the Institutional Revolutionary Party could lose control of the lower house of Congress for the first time since 1929.
((--Elena Vega, Mexico City Newsroom 525 728-9554)) (c) Reuters Limited 1997
